Overview of the Action Plan The Action Plan outlines the strategic plan of the Department for the next six years including annual benchmarks used to assess progress. The plan addresses major issues raised in the self- study and by the external reviewer(s), and relates these to the strategic plan of the Department. The plan also includes specific goals, their rationale, and estimates of resources required. ● Faculty review and discuss the external reviewer’s self-study, and the Department Chair collaborates with the faculty to develop a draft Action Plan that is submitted to the Dean. ● The Dean meets with the Department chair (and/or the self-study chair, if a different person) to develop a mutually agreeable proposed Action Plan that is submitted to the Provost with the Self-Study and the External Reviewer Report. ● The Department chair, the Dean, the Provost and representatives from the Provost’s office meet to discuss the Action Plan for the Department which outlines the strategic plan for the next six years, addressing any major issues raised in the self-study and external review, and includes specific goals and resource estimates. ● To promote continuous quality improvement, the Provost may request a follow up, Interim Report from the department. Interim reports will be submitted to the Dean who will present them to the Provost for discussion. ● The approved Action Plan is complete following this discussion and represents an agreement between the Department, the college Dean, and the Provost for actions to be taken over time, benchmarks used to assess progress, and a plan for allocation of resources. 40

Action Plan Guidelines Action Plan Development, Milestones and Implementation Plan Action Planning is a continuous and multi-year process. See the table below for a detailed timeline of milestones associated with Action Plan Development and Implementation. Timeline Activity Description Initial Development Year 1, Months 1-3 Faculty Engagement Faculty review and discuss the findings from the external review and the self-study, kickstarting the development of the Action Plan. Year 1, Months 4-6 Drafting the Plan The Department Chair collaborates with faculty to create a draft Action Plan. This draft is then submitted to the Dean for initial feedback. Review and Approval Process Year 1, Months 7-9 Collaborative Refinement The Dean and the Department Chair (including the self-study chair if different) refine the draft Action Plan into a mutually agreeable proposal. Year 1, Month 10 Strategic Submission This proposed Action Plan, together with the Self-Study and the External Reviewer Report, is submitted to the Provost for preliminary approval. Year 1, Months 11-12 Comprehensive Discussion The Department Chair, Dean, Provost, and representatives from the Provost’s office meet to discuss, finalize, and approve the Action Plan. Implementation and Monitoring Year 2-5 Action The approved Action Plan is implemented, 41

Implementation setting the course for the department’s actions. Departments initiate projects and strategies outlined in the plan and start monitoring their impact. Year 2-5 Regular Monitoring Departments conduct annual reviews to monitor progress against the benchmarks set in the Action Plan. Adjustments are made based on these reviews to ensure the plan remains responsive to both achievements and challenges. Goals and progress toward goals are discussed annually with the Dean. Year 6 Evaluation and Preparation for Next Cycle A comprehensive evaluation of the Action Plan’s outcomes is conducted to assess its effectiveness and gather insights for the next APR cycle. This evaluation informs the upcoming self-study and the development of a new Action Plan. Cycle Repeats Year 6, Months 1-3 Start New Cycle The next cycle begins with updated orientation and data collection, reflecting the latest developments and priorities in the department’s discipline and the broader institutional context. 42

2025-26 Academic Year Annual Report of the Joint Committee for Academic Program Review & Outcomes Assessment to the Faculty Senate May 2026 The 2026 update on learning outcomes assessment (2025-2026 academic assessment reporting year) reaffirms that student learning outcomes and academic program assessment is acknowledged as a shared responsibility and demonstrates a regular and ongoing commitment to understanding student learning and student success.
Data and results from outcomes assessment activities are examined in the aggregate only and are not used to evaluate individual faculty nor students, but to improve learning opportunities for all students.
This report is submitted by the Office of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation in the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning , and in partial fulfillment of the charge outlined for the Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment ( JCAPROA , Spring 2024).

Item #3: Student Learning Outcomes Assessment Process Review and Update For years, the Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation team in the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning has provided support to all URI colleges and departments as it relates to the effective evaluation of student learning outcomes in the undergraduate curriculum.
Historically, the evaluation of student learning outcomes at URI happened on a 2-year cycle, until the fall of 2024 when the university’s largest college, the College of Arts & Sciences, was collaboratively shifted by request to a 3-year cycle.
Since then, our team has listened to other university leaders (Deans, Associate Deans, and Department Chairs, and individual faculty) from other colleges across URI regarding this topic.
During the fall 2025 semester, members of our team reached out to more than 50 other universities to learn more about their 1 Not all programs will have completed the approval process at the time of this update. 1

assessment processes.
From those conversations, along with receiving support from the Office of the Provost, we worked during the 2025-2026 academic year to reset the university’s undergraduate academic program assessment cycle to a 3-year schedule.
A timeline of those events is below.

Timeline ● Fall 2023: The College of Arts & Sciences petitioned the Provost’s Office for an additional year to be added to the undergraduate assessment cycle in order to complete a deeper and richer analysis of the student learning outcomes across programs in the college. ● Fall 2023: Conversations were ongoing to identify a positive solution to the opportunity raised by the CAS. ● Spring 2024: The Provost’s Office supported the proposed additional year, and a pilot began during the Fall 2024 semester. ● Fall 2024: The College of Arts and Sciences 3-y pilot assessment cycle begins. ● Spring 2025: Other college leaders begin to see the benefits of moving to a 3-year cycle and they express their desire to move to a 3-year cycle. ● Fall 2025: The undergraduate academic program assessment cycle schedule is paused to allow the Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA) team time to research the potential implications for a university-wide change in the assessment schedule, The SLOAA team contacts more than 50 universities to learn more about their assessment cycles for evaluating student learning outcomes. ● Spring 2026: The updated 3-year cycle is supported by the Office of the Provost, and the updated cycle is shared with the university.

DISCUSSION ITEMS a.
Review of Preliminary FY2026 Year-End Numbers Enclosure Abby Benson, Senior Vice President, Administration and Finance The Finance and Facilities Committee members reviewed the FY26 year-end numbers as presented by Senior Vice President for Administration and Finance Abby Benson.
These figures show a $2.2 million shortfall in the unrestricted budget, less than the budgeted $3.8 million shortfall.
The variance was attributed to a combination of overbudget utilities expenses (which included fewer solar credits than expected and also Rhode Island Energy billing abnormalities during the year) and lower tuition due to fewer continuing students, which was offset somewhat by online programs revenue, higher-than- expected interest income, and careful position management within the University throughout the year.
Senior Vice President Benson noted that the New Budget Model is now in place for FY27 and efforts at this time are focused on policy and guidance development for subvention and reserve management.

She reminded the Committee that the University completed a Balanced Budget Initiative during FY26 to better align historical spend with the budget for future year requests.
There were no questions from the Committee. b.
Update on Workday Implementation Enclosure Abby Benson, Senior Vice President, Administration and Finance Senior Vice President Benson introduced Stephanie Cavanagh, the University’s Workday Program Director, who is leading the implementation effort.
Stephanie Cavanagh provided an update on URI's Workday implementation project, confirming that the project remains on track with its fixed-fee LaunchFlex methodology approach.
The implementation is currently in the architect and configure stage, with testing scheduled to begin in December and continue through August 2027, ahead of a planned October 2027 launch.
Trustees discussed the primary project risk and learned that integration with the state’s Workday system remains the greatest concern, as ongoing state payroll issues could affect URI’s implementation.
URI continues to meet regularly with state leadership to address this concern. 3.

She noted that Associate Vice President John Poehlmann has led the effort for the development of the budget, as he has done in previous years.
This presentation focused primarily on the state appropriation portion of the University budget.
Senior Vice President Benson first compared the FY27 request ($156.7 million) to the FY27 enacted budget ($124.5 million), noting the breakdown of the request, including $5.0 million for Medical School planning.
Benson also discussed the all-funds FY27 revenue budget before moving on to a discussion of the FY28 budget submission, showing all projected sources and uses of funds.
Senior Vice President Benson then provided the assumptions regarding enrollment, tuition rates, and fees used in developing the FY28 budget, noting a small increase in undergraduate enrollment (<1%), a small decrease (1%) in graduate enrollment, and a 3% increase in tuition and fees.

Benson emphasized that these figures are for planning purposes only; the actual request for changes to tuition and fees will be brought to the Board in February.
She also discussed challenges to continued growth in undergraduate enrollment.
Senior Vice President Benson then discussed the FY28 State Appropriation request of $139.8 million (not including the medical school request of $7.0 million).
She noted that the University is planning for an $8.1 million budgeted operating shortfall.
The University is requesting a total of $146.8 million in state appropriations, including $7 million for the second year of medical school planning, which is presented separately from the University’s operating budget.
Benson also discussed the details within the Current Service Level request, including the largest portion related to Cost-of-Living Adjustments (COLA), a strategic increase in financial aid, a $5.0 million anticipated savings though position management, additional funds to aid URI Athletics operations, and additional funds to cover increased utilities costs.

Closing the presentation, Senior Vice President Benson discussed future year budget strategies, noting the University’s focus on enrollment strategies that emphasize new offerings and modalities, an increased focus on revenue generating opportunities, the ongoing careful management of staffing levels, and continued efforts to improve operational efficiency.
Senior Vice President Benson addressed Trustee Bovy’s inquiry about the state’s recent authorization increasing URI’s full time equivalent (FTE) employee cap.
Benson noted that, given ongoing financial pressures and personnel costs representing the University’s largest expense, URI is evaluating potential adjustments to the hiring process as it plans for FY2028.
The University intends to retain enhanced oversight of hiring to help control operating budget shortfalls.
President Parlange noted that the FTE restrictions apply to the unrestricted operating budget (Fund 100), with separate carve-outs for auxiliary operations, including housing and dining, as well as grant-funded research and sponsored programs.

Responding to trustee inquiry about the state’s funding of the proposed medical school at URI, Benson confirmed that there is legislative intent to provide an additional $7 million in FY 2028 and $8 million in FY 2029 to continue development of the state’s only public medical school.
Hearing no further questions, Committee Chair Ownjazayeri called for a motion; on a motion duly made by Armand Sabitoni, and seconded by David Barrett, and hearing no discussion, it was VOTED: THAT the Committee recommend approval of the University’s FY2028 Total
